source.title: Block-Recurrent Transformers
source.authors: DeLesley S. Hutchins; Imanol Schlag; Yu-Huai Wu; Ethan Dyer; Behnam Neyshabur

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a parameter-scale sweep of held-out language-model loss, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.gate_note: The paper's own PG19 scaling sweep reports test bits-per-token for six parameter sizes in two model configurations. It does not fit a power law or test predictions from small runs. The Chinchilla scaling study and other cited scaling findings are background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. Its only scale sweep (Table 4/Fig. 3: six PG19 models, 40.6M–1.3B params) exists to show that recurrence beats Transformer-XL at every size. No power law is fitted, there is no extrapolation, and tokens and compute are not varied. The sweep spans about 1.5 orders of magnitude, and depth changes between the 325M and 650M points (12/13 to 24/26 layers), so it cannot test V1's form. The scaling-law statements in C.3 cite prior work (Chinchilla).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that recurrence beats Transformer-XL at every tested scale, with a benefit that seems to grow with size. At larger sizes it exceeds the benefit of doubling parameters. They note that larger models do better, and caution that vocabulary, learning-rate schedule, batch size, training steps and optimizer affect perplexity, so cross-paper comparisons need controls.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a parameter sweep of Block-Recurrent Transformers and Transformer-XL models on PG19, rather than fitting and evaluating the original scaling-law equations. It does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says learning-rate schedule and vocabulary affect final loss; its vocabulary ablation varies tokenization, and its discussion cautions that several training choices affect perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: PG19 test bits-per-token falls monotonically with parameter count for both architectures. For XL the gains per doubling are 0.17, 0.19, 0.16, 0.12, 0.08, shrinking at the largest sizes; there is no fit, and depth changes at 650M. The recurrence advantage grows from 0.07 to about 0.09–0.10 bits at the two largest sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural improvements (recurrence) give a constant or growing loss offset across parameter scales, equivalent to more than doubling parameters.

record.problems: The parameter-sweep table reports no uncertainty estimates. The study does not fit a functional scaling law, test extrapolation, or control all training variables across published comparisons. The authors state that not all experiments were repeated and that error bars are unavailable for some experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 architecture/gating comparisons are not parameter-scaling results. The vocabulary ablation in Appendix I reports tokenizer-dependent loss values but does not measure scaling exponents or compute allocation, so it is not included as a claim-version row. Cited results about scaling laws are not this study's own findings.

untested.parts: No power-law fit. Only about 1.5 orders of magnitude of parameters, with depth changed mid-sweep and fixed training steps. No token or compute scaling.
No downstream tasks; listed as future work.
No exponent fits or comparison of fitting choices. The finding that the learning-rate schedule and vocabulary change loss concerns absolute loss, not fitted laws.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification overstates the study. The scaling sweep is a vehicle for comparing architectures. The rows pair architectures at equal size, so none measures V1's loss-vs-scale relationship.

versions.untested_parts: Only parameter scaling is swept, on PG19, in the reported model configurations. The paper does not fit or establish a power-law form, test token or compute scaling, or establish that other variables are not bottlenecks.
No predictions from power-law fits on small runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trends are measured.
The paper does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested for the same power-law form.
No downstream task performance is measured against scale or pretraining loss; downstream evaluation is described as future work.

The paper does not fit or compare scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, or power-law curves under different fitting choices. It does report that tokenizer and training-schedule choices affect loss measurements.
